slide.titolo: Il rapporto CNN sui piani iraniani
slide.testo: Secondo CNN, nuova intelligence Usa indica che l'Iran sta preparando piani per colpire alti funzionari dell'amministrazione Trump a Washington con una bomba sporca o un'arma chimica. Le fonti sono sette funzionari anonimi. BBC e CNBC non hanno verificato il rapporto.
Se c'è, pagheranno un prezzo che nessun paese ha mai pagato prima. Spero di no, ma lo prendiamo molto sul serio, perché sono pazzi.
slide.autore: Donald Trump, presidente degli Stati Uniti, al vertice Asean nelle Filippine

slide.testo: La portavoce Lauren Bis: «Al momento non ci sono minacce credibili al territorio nazionale». Secondo le fonti CNN, i piani servono a Teheran per «darsi opzioni», non indicano un attacco imminente. I funzionari Usa discutono se l'Iran potrebbe o vorrebbe davvero agire.

Il portavoce degli Esteri Esmail Baghaei accusa chi ha «avviato l'aggressione» di preparare il terreno mediatico con «accuse infondate». La missione iraniana all'Onu «respinge categoricamente» le accuse, definite false e fabbricate.

Non è un'arma nucleare. Secondo la National Academy of Sciences Usa, contaminerebbe subito uno o due isolati. Nel 2002 l'allora capo della Commissione nucleare Usa stimò i morti nell'ordine delle decine. Gli esperti la chiamano «arma di distruzione di massa». No: «di disturbo di massa».

slide.titolo: Trattative ferme, tre portaerei Usa nell'area
slide.testo: Secondo Al Jazeera, i negoziati per chiudere la guerra Usa-Israele contro l'Iran, iniziata a febbraio, sono in stallo. È appena arrivata la portaerei USS Theodore Roosevelt: ora gli Usa ne hanno tre nella regione, con timori di nuova escalation.

c.perche_ti_riguarda: Secondo il Guardian, il blocco iraniano dello Stretto di Hormuz ha già fatto salire i costi del carburante e scosso l'economia globale. Una nuova escalation tra Usa e Iran potrebbe pesare ancora su prezzi dell'energia e pieni.

sources.title: Trump claims US is ‘looking into’ Iranian bomb plot in Washington despite ‘no credible threats’
sources.text:
Donald Trump has claimed the US is “looking into” whether Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, even as the White House said there are “no credible threats” at this time.
Trump said his administration takes the idea “very seriously”
After a CNN report, citing seven unnamed US officials, that new US intelligence suggested Iran was working on plans that would use a dirty bomb, which combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, or a chemical weapon against senior Trump administration officials.
The report noted, however, that US officials “continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute such a plot”.
The US president’s war on Iran is deeply unpopular among Americans. His Republican party was widely rejected by voters in the midterm elections, in which the GOP lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives.
Asked in the Philippines on Tuesday if there was reason to believe that such an Iranian attack was imminent, Trump said: “If there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement: “We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”
CNN cited the unnamed officials as saying that Tehran’s planning was an effort by Iran to “give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack”, but the plans include specific locations and targets.
While the plans would signify that Iran is willing to escalate its tactics against the US, there is no evidence to suggest they will go ahead with them.
The US and Israel went to war with Iran starting in February, with early airstrikes killing Iranian officials, including supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Trump has repeatedly claimed the war will be over soon, but it has continued.
The US president has argued that US involvement in the war is necessary so that the country doesn’t build nuclear weapons. Iran has blocked trade through the strait of Hormuz, creating rising fuel costs – and rattling the global economy.

sources.title: Trump on Iran's reported DC dirty bomb plan: 'We take it very seriously'
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that if a report about Iran developing plans to target top administration officials with a "dirty bomb" in Washington is true, Iran would face consequences.
"Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before," Trump said when asked if there is any imminent threat to Washington, D.C., home to close to 700,000 people in addition to the seat of government.
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously, because they happen to be crazy," Trump said during a photo-op with world leaders at the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, Philippines.
"This is why they can't have a nuclear weapon, by the way, in case people had any questions," Trump added, reiterating his main defense for launching a war with Iran in late February.
Late Monday, CNN cited two U.S. officials in reporting that new U.S. intelligence has intercepted "very specific" plans, including "locations and targets," related to a potential Iranian plot to set off a dirty bomb, which combines conventional explosives with radioactive material.
Officials have debated whether Iran would actually attempt to detonate such a device in the U.S., or even if it could, CNN reported, citing seven U.S. officials in total.
CNBC has not verified the report. Trump administration spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CNN in a statement that the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Trump was asked about imminent Iranian threats during the first leg of his tour through Asia, which begins at ASEAN and is set to include high-stakes meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Asked about the dirty bomb report on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday morning, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested the Iranian plot was not new and described Tehran as "aspirational" in its threats.
If Iran were to take such an action, "you would cause an all-out war" with the U.S., which would attack at such a level that the Islamic Republic's allies, such as China and Russia, would not come to its aid, Mullin said.
It is a threat, and "we take it very serious," he added. "But the homeland is secure, I can tell you that. But every day we addressing new threats."
CNN reported later Tuesday morning that NSA Net, the classified communications network used by the National Security Agency, is down, citing six people familiar with the matter.

sources.title: Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington
sources.text:
Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington
- Published
President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.
In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it."
CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack.
Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred.
Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated.
The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting.
During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent.
"I hope it's not," he said, "but we take it very seriously because they [the Iranians] happen to be crazy."
In a statement before Trump's comments, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote: "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rebutted the CNN article and other US reports.
He posted on X: "Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations."
Mick Mulroy, a former CIA paramilitary officer and deputy assistant defence secretary, told the BBC: "A dirty bomb is not difficult to make or deploy."
"Although it is not a weapon of mass destruction, it can be a weapon of mass disruption," he added.
Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, said that it remains "unclear how serious" would be the threat of a supposed Iranian dirty bomb.
"But Iran has planned and threatened to attack the US in the past," he said. "It is also unclear why this report is becoming public now."
It comes as intelligence officials and members of the Trump administration seek congressional renewal of a key national security law.
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), which allows the US to âspy on foreign nationals, expires next March.

sources.title: Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know
sources.text:
Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know
A CNN report quoting unnamed US officials alleges Tehran is developing plans for an attack on officials in Washington, DC.
CNN has reported that United States intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior officials in President Donald Trump’s administration with a “dirty bomb” or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC. The broadcaster quotes seven unnamed US officials.
However, the report sets out no evidence to support the claims.
According to CNN, its sources described the planning as an effort by Tehran to give itself options, not as an imminent attack. One source said US intelligence had picked up Iranian “chatter” indicating that bomb-making materials had been stashed inside the US. That claim has not been independently verified.
The White House said it was “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time, there are no credible threats to the homeland”. Iran’s mission to the United Nations said Tehran “categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations”.
The report was released as talks to end the US-Israel war on Iran have stalled and Trump said last week that Washington does not “need” a deal. The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt has just arrived in the region, bringing the number of US carriers there to three and adding to fears of a renewed escalation.
So what is a dirty bomb? Could Iran build one? And how seriously should the latest claims be taken?
What is a ‘dirty bomb’?
A dirty bomb, technically known as a radiological dispersal device, combines conventional explosives, such as dynamite, with radioactive material. When the bomb explodes, the resulting blast scatters the radioactive material into the surrounding area.
Unlike a nuclear weapon, a dirty bomb does not need enriched uranium or a nuclear chain reaction. The radioactive material can come from medical or industrial equipment, such as machines used in hospitals and research facilities. That makes a dirty bomb far cheaper and easier to build than a nuclear device. It is also far less destructive.
The main health risk comes from breathing in contaminated dust near the blast. As the material spreads, it becomes less concentrated and less harmful. The damage depends on the size of the explosive charge, the type and amount of radioactive material and the weather, especially the wind.
According to the US National Academy of Sciences, most dirty bombs would immediately contaminate an area of one or two city blocks although wind could carry radioactive particles over a few square miles.
Experts said dirty bombs are unlikely to cause mass casualties. In testimony to the US Senate in 2002, Richard Meserve, then-chairman of the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, estimated that deaths in most scenarios would be in the tens, not the hundreds or thousands.
“It’s important to understand that a dirty bomb isn’t an off-the-shelf nuclear bomb. There aren’t any mushroom clouds and massive shockwaves tearing down buildings and killing hundreds of thousands of people in the blink of an eye,” Talha Abdulrazaq, a researcher at the University of Exeter’s Strategy and Security Institute told Al Jazeera. “Instead, its primary effect would be psychological panic and hysteria in the target state alongside radioactive contamination, turning the area hit into a no-go zone.”
That is why experts call dirty bombs “weapons of mass disruption” rather than weapons of mass destruction.
Does Iran have the ability to build one?
In theory, yes. But so do many states and armed groups.
A dirty bomb is “really easy to make”, Scott Roecker, vice president for nuclear materials security at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, told Al Jazeera in 2022. Radioactive sources used in medicine and industry can be found in many countries and building a crude device does not require advanced technical knowledge.
Iran has a large civilian nuclear programme. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency’s last assessment, it held about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent as of June 2025.
In an April analysis for the European Council on Foreign Relations, Jacek Siewiera, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote that although the stockpile falls short of what is needed for a nuclear weapon, it “could be extraordinarily dangerous from a radiological and sabotage perspective”. He warned that a dirty bomb could be “either a deliberate element of escalation or an unintended consequence of weakened central control” because international institutions no longer know who controls Iran’s nuclear storage sites.
But even enriched uranium is only weakly radioactive, which makes it a poor choice for a dirty bomb. Many analysts also argued that Tehran would be unlikely to waste material it spent decades producing.
A June 2025 analysis by Chris Kremidas-Courtney for the Euro-Atlantic Resilience Centre, a Bucharest-based think tank, reached a similar conclusion.
Iran is “widely believed to have access to sufficient radioactive material for use in dirty bombs, particularly from civilian nuclear and industrial sources”, he wrote. He pointed to isotopes such as caesium-137, used in cancer treatment, and cobalt-60, used in industrial radiography.
Kremidas-Courtney, however, described a dirty bomb as a possible “tool of last resort under extreme circumstances”. He also judged that the US “poses a high bar for direct infiltration” and ports and maritime chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz, were more plausible targets.
Building a dirty bomb “is actually far easier than a conventional nuclear weapon” and does not require highly enriched uranium, Abdulrazaq said. Even after US strikes on the Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities, “a degraded capability doesn’t mean a destroyed capability,” he told Al Jazeera. “Iran certainly has access to all the components and expertise required to construct something as rudimentary as a dirty bomb.”

Inflazione in Italia al 5,5% a ottobre, il livello più alto da oltre tre anni

Secondo il dato definitivo dell'Istat, i prezzi al consumo sono saliti del 5,5% su base annua, oltre la stima preliminare del 5,4% e in netto rialzo dal 4,2% di settembre. c.titolo_copertina: Inflazione al 5,5%: prezzi ai massimi da oltre tre anni, energia +31,9%

slide.titolo: Ottobre, l'inflazione supera anche le stime
slide.testo: Secondo il dato definitivo Istat, i prezzi al consumo salgono del 5,5% in un anno e dell'1% in un mese. La stima preliminare era del 5,4%. A settembre il dato era +4,2%.
I beni energetici passano da +22,6% a +31,9%, influenzati dal quadro geopolitico, spiega l'Istat. I beni regolamentati arrivano a +61,6% annuo, con un balzo del 20,3% in un solo mese.

Il carrello della spesa sale da +1,5% a +2,3%. Gli acquisti ad alta frequenza a +5,8%. Rincari annui: pomodori +52,6%, fragole +41,3%, carciofi +31,4%, insalata +13,7%, uova +7,4%. Trasporti raddoppiati: da +1,6% a +3,2%.
Secondo Unc e Codacons, per una coppia con due figli il carovita supera ampiamente i 2.000 euro l'anno. In testa ai rincari mensili, per Unc, l'elettricità del mercato tutelato: +34,1%.
Questa fiammata dell'inflazione rischia di compromettere le prospettive dei consumi e della crescita.

slide.titolo: Pressing sul governo, si teme il Natale
slide.testo: Assoutenti chiede al governo di tagliare subito Iva e oneri di sistema in bolletta per alleggerire la spesa invernale del gas. Il Codacons avverte: in arrivo una stangata di Natale.

c.perche_ti_riguarda: Benzina, bollette, trasporti e spesa costano di più. Per una famiglia con due figli l'aggravio stimato dalle associazioni supera i 2.000 euro l'anno. E secondo il Codacons i prossimi mesi non andranno meglio.

sources.title: I prezzi volano oltre le stime, ad ottobre +5,5%
sources.text:
I prezzi volano e per le famiglie italiane far benzina all'auto, spostarsi, pagare bollette o fare la spesa di tutti i giorni diventa sempre più oneroso. Con aggravi per i bilanci personali che rischiano di arrivare addirittura a superare i 2.000 all'anno. E' questo l'esito di una nuova fiammata dell'inflazione, che a ottobre è salita al livello più alto da oltre tre anni superando anche le stime preliminari avanzate dall'Istat alla fine del mese scorso.
Sotto la spinta soprattutto dei rincari dei prodotti energetici, degli alimentari e di servizi essenziali quali i trasporti, il dato definitivo di ottobre registra un aumento dei prezzi al consumo dell'1% su base mensile e del 5,5% in un anno, contro la stima preliminare del 5,4% e ben oltre il +4,2% di settembre.
L'Istat spiega che la corsa dell'inflazione risente principalmente del rialzo dei beni energetici, da +22,6% a +31,9%, ancora influenzato dal quadro geopolitico internazionale. Un contributo si deve poi agli alimentari non lavorati (da +5,5% a +7,5%) e ai trasporti, raddoppiati da +1,6% a +3,2%.
Tra gli energetici in particolare, a rendere i dati definitivi più pesanti delle stime sono stati soprattutto i beni regolamentati, la cui crescita tendenziale è passata dal +59,5% preliminare a +61,6% (da +25,8% di settembre), con un balzo del 20,3% in un solo mese. Il contagio non risparmia tuttavia la vita quotidiana e i beni essenziali: il carrello della spesa, che mette insieme beni alimentari, per la cura della casa e della persona è infatti salito dal +1,5% di settembre a +2,3%. Mentre i prodotti ad alta frequenza d'acquisto, le spese obbligate di tutti i giorni, vanno al +5,8% dal precedente +5,2% precedente.
L'allarme prezzi si fa sentire tra i consumatori. Al pari del Codacons anche Unc calcola ad esempio che per una coppia con 2 figli la stangata dovuta al carovita supera ampiamente la soglia dei 2.000 euro, mentre indica al primo posto nella top ten dei rincari mensili l'elettricità per il mercato tutelato, con +34,1%. L'Adusbef fa notare che la voce alimentari e bevande analcoliche registra un'inflazione del +2,7% che, a parità di consumi, equivale ad un aggravio di spesa da complessivi 4,8 miliardi di euro in un anno solo per cibi e bevande.
Effettivamente sono molti gli alimenti di largo consumo i cui prezzi stanno registrando rincari record: i pomodori aumentano in media del 52,6% su base annua, le fragole del 41,3%, i carciofi del 31,4%, cavolfiori e broccoli +14,8%, l'insalata del +13,7%, le arance segnano un +9,5%, le patate +7,8% e le uova +7,4%. Ma nei prossimi mesi non andrà meglio: secondo il Codacons gli italiani devono prepararsi ad una stangata di Natale determinata dai forti rincari di prezzi e tariffe che stanno caratterizzando i diversi comparti.
Assoutenti chiede al governo di intervenire subito disponendo un taglio dell'Iva e degli oneri di sistema in bolletta, in modo da alleggerire almeno la spesa invernale delle famiglie per i consumi di gas. Un grido di allarme arriva anche dal mondo del commercio. La nuova fiammata dell' inflazione "rischia di compromettere le prospettive dei consumi e della crescita" avverte Confesercenti che ritiene perciò "essenziale concentrare le risorse disponibili sul contrasto al caro energia e sul sostegno al potere d'acquisto".
